content: The document titled Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region (September 2023) provides comprehensive guidance on the surveillance and management of CRS. It emphasizes the importance of CRS surveillance as a critical component of rubella vaccination programs, aiming to prevent the severe outcomes of rubella infection during pregnancy. Below is a professional summary of the key points: 1. Introduction to CRS Surveillance: Rubella surveillance alone cannot capture all cases due to the mild or asymptomatic nature of the disease. CRS, the most severe outcome of rubella infection, is the primary target for prevention through vaccination. Surveillance of CRS enables the detection of infants with clinical manifestations, facilitates early intervention, and supports regional and global reporting. 2. Objectives of CRS Surveillance: The primary goal is to provide data to support national rubella vaccination goals, monitor progress toward disease elimination, and mitigate the consequences of CRS through early medical care. Specific objectives include monitoring the impact of rubella vaccination, rapid detection and isolation of affected infants, and demonstrating the elimination of rubella and CRS. 3. Separate Surveillance for Rubella and CRS: Although rubella and CRS are linked, their surveillance systems differ significantly in case definitions, target age groups, and detection sites. Member States in the South-East Asia Region are encouraged to develop CRS surveillance systems that capture most suspected cases. Countries without existing systems may start with sentinel sites and expand coverage over time. 4. Types of Surveillance: Minimal Surveillance: Case-based surveillance at sentinel sites with laboratory confirmation is recommended, targeting infants under 12 months of age. Enhanced Surveillance: A national case-based system (passive, active, or both) with laboratory confirmation is advised for broader coverage. 5. Case Detection and Definitions: Health workers should suspect CRS in infants under 12 months with congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, or specific eye abnormalities (e.g., cataracts, glaucoma). CRS should also be suspected in infants born to mothers with confirmed or suspected rubella infection during pregnancy. 6. Case Reporting and Investigation: Passive reporting from sentinel sites is the most common method. Secondary and tertiary care facilities, such as pediatric and obstetric centers, are ideal reporting sites. A nodal person should coordinate data collection, specimen transport, and communication with national coordinators. Suspected cases must be investigated within 48 hours, and a unique case identification number (UID) should be assigned. 7. Specimen Collection and Laboratory Testing: Specimens for virus detection (e.g., nasopharyngeal swabs, urine) and antibody testing (e.g., blood samples) are critical for laboratory confirmation. Infants under six months are tested for rubella IgM antibodies, while older infants may require additional IgG testing or viral isolation. 8. Case Management: There is no specific treatment for CRS beyond managing congenital abnormalities. Follow-up care should be provided by experienced personnel according to national guidelines. 9. Outbreak Response: An increase in CRS cases often follows a rubella outbreak. Surveillance should be strengthened in affected areas, and active case-finding should be conducted. 10. Special Considerations: Retrospective reviews of medical records can help monitor surveillance sensitivity and estimate disease burden. Serological surveys among women of reproductive age can assess population immunity but are not a substitute for CRS surveillance. 11. Data Management and Reporting: CRS cases should be reported separately from rubella cases. Data should include demographic, clinical, and laboratory information, as well as maternal history. 12. Public Health Response: Infants with CRS or congenital rubella infection (CRI) should be considered infectious until two negative viral tests are obtained. Community-based active searches and vaccination campaigns are recommended in outbreak settings. This guide underscores the importance of robust CRS surveillance systems to achieve and maintain rubella elimination goals, protect public health, and provide timely care for affected infants.
